title: Sweaty and silent
intro:
Mrs. Lourdes Navarro, 63, has had type 2 diabetes for 15 years and takes insulin. She dialyzes on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays through a left arm fistula. Today is Tuesday, the first session after the long weekend gap. She had only coffee this morning because she felt unwell, but she took her usual insulin.

At hour 0:45 the nurse, Ms. Carmela Ramos, calls you. Mrs. Navarro has stopped answering questions and is sweating. Both needles are in place, the blood pump is running, and there are no machine alarms. Her predialysis potassium was sent at 6:30 a.m. and has not come back.

n1.prompt: After a glance at her airway and breathing, what do you check first?

choices.feedback: She took insulin, ate nothing, and is losing glucose into the dialysis fluid. A failed kidney also clears insulin slowly. Low sugar is the likeliest cause of confusion and sweating here, and the fastest to reverse. It takes one minute.

choices.text: A full stroke check of face, arm, and speech, and the time she was last seen well.
choices.feedback: Stroke matters in a confused dialysis patient, and you will record when she was last seen well. But a glucose comes first, because low sugar can mimic a stroke and is reversible in minutes.
choices.then: Her face and arms are hard to assess while she is not following commands. Ms. Ramos checks the glucose: 44 mg/dL.

choices.text: Have the session stopped and send her to the emergency department for a head CT.
choices.feedback: Sending her out before a one-minute bedside test skips the most likely, reversible cause. Hypoglycemia left untreated during transfer can cause brain injury.
choices.then: Ms. Ramos asks to check a glucose before the transfer. It is 44 mg/dL.

n2.scene: Ms. Ramos treats the low sugar under the unit’s protocol. Within minutes Mrs. Navarro wakes, apologizes, and asks for her daughter. Her recheck is 112 mg/dL. Then the laboratory calls: her predialysis potassium is 6.8 mmol/L. The monitor shows tall, narrow T waves, and her pulse is 56.
n2.prompt: How do you rank what is in front of you?

choices.text: Two problems: low sugar caused the confusion; the potassium is now the bigger danger.
choices.feedback: High potassium causes weakness and rhythm problems, rarely confusion, and the quick recovery with sugar confirms the cause. A potassium of 6.8 with peaked T waves and a slow pulse can stop the heart without warning.

choices.text: One problem: the potassium caused the confusion, and the low sugar was a coincidence that is now fixed.
choices.feedback: Her prompt recovery after glucose shows the low sugar caused the confusion. Merging the two risks missing the next low sugar, especially if insulin is about to be used.

choices.text: She is awake now, so the crisis is over. Note the potassium and review it after dialysis.
choices.feedback: The ECG changes and slow pulse mean the potassium is acting on the heart now. Waiting until the end of the session leaves her exposed to a rhythm arrest.

n3.prompt: What do you do about the potassium?

choices.text: Monitor, calcium for the ECG changes, the order set, dialysis running, and call.
choices.feedback: Stabilize, shift, remove. Calcium protects the heart muscle without lowering potassium. Dialysis is the treatment that removes it, and she is already connected. The nephrologist needs the value, the ECG, and the fact that she was hypoglycemic minutes ago.

choices.text: Stop dialysis and transfer her to the emergency department, where hyperkalemia can be treated with full monitoring.
choices.feedback: Dialysis is the definitive treatment for high potassium, and she is already on it. Stopping it to transfer her removes the one step that lowers total body potassium.
choices.then: You keep her connected, give calcium under the order set, and call the attending nephrologist.

choices.text: Keep dialysis running and recheck the potassium in an hour.
choices.feedback: Keeping dialysis running is right. But ECG changes with a slow pulse call for calcium under the order set now, plus a monitor and an immediate call, not a wait.
choices.then: You give calcium under the order set and call the attending nephrologist.

n4.scene: The attending nephrologist agrees with your plan and decides, under the order set, to add insulin with glucose while dialysis continues.
n4.prompt: What must happen over the next several hours?

choices.text: Glucose checks for hours, past the end of dialysis; she eats; home only when the attending agrees.
choices.feedback: In hospital series, hypoglycemia after insulin for hyperkalemia began at a median of about 2 hours and lasted about 2 hours. Mrs. Navarro is at higher risk: she was already low, has not eaten, and her own insulin is still acting.

choices.text: One glucose check 30 minutes after the insulin; if it is normal, no further checks.
choices.feedback: A single early check misses most of the risk window, which runs for hours. A normal value at 30 minutes says little about 2 hours.

choices.text: Glucose checks every 30 minutes until the end of dialysis, when the insulin effect will have worn off.
choices.feedback: The checks need to continue past the end of the session if the window has not passed. The schedule and amounts come from the order set, which the Medical Director sets.

n5.scene: The session ends. Her potassium is 4.6 mmol/L, her glucose 98 mg/dL, and the ECG has improved. Her daughter is waiting to take her home.
n5.prompt: What do you do before she leaves?

choices.text: Confirm she ate and the watch window passed, give warning signs, and report.
choices.feedback: Potassium rebounds after the session as cells release it, and sugar can fall again at home. The nephrologist decides whether she may go and reviews her home insulin, which was given on an empty stomach before dialysis.

choices.text: Her numbers are normal now, so she can go.
choices.feedback: Normal numbers at the end of dialysis do not cover the next few hours. The insulin may still be acting, and potassium rebounds. She goes home only when the nephrologist agrees.

choices.text: Keep her for one more glucose check after dialysis, and send her home if it is normal.
choices.feedback: An extra check is reasonable. But the decision to send her home, and changes to her home insulin, belong to the attending nephrologist.

end.title: Home, with a plan
end.text: Mrs. Navarro eats, her glucose stays in range through the watch window, and the attending nephrologist agrees she may go home with her daughter. The nephrologist will review her insulin on dialysis days. You write the times, the glucose readings, the potassium and ECG, the treatments given under the order set, the advice received, and her condition when she left.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Check the sugar first in any confused, sweaty, or drowsy dialysis patient. Only airway, breathing, and circulation come before it.
  • Two problems can arrive together. The low sugar explained the confusion; the high potassium with ECG changes was the bigger threat.
  • Stabilize, shift, remove. Calcium for ECG changes, shifting agents per the order set, and dialysis, which is the treatment and keeps running.
  • Insulin outlasts the glucose given with it in kidney failure. Glucose checks run for hours, past the end of the session.

See the lesson parts Stabilize, shift, remove and Sugar falls in the chair.
